entities.name: Conrad of Vechta
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Conrad of Vechta, who died on January 2, 1432, was a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in late medieval Central Europe, whose career spanned key bishoprics and the chancellorship of Bohemia amidst the burgeoning Hussite movement. His trajectory from Bishop of Verden to Archbishop of Prague, coupled with his significant administrative roles in the Kingdom of Bohemia, placed him at the heart of the complex religious and political struggles that defined the early 15th century, particularly the initial phases of the Hussite Wars.

Beginning his episcopal career as Bishop of Verden (1400–1402/1407), Conrad quickly ascended, becoming Bishop of Olomouc (1408–1413) before his elevation to Archbishop of Prague in 1413. Simultaneously, he served the Bohemian Crown as Master of the Mint (1401–1403) and, most notably, as Chancellor (1405–1412), a position of immense influence within the royal court. His archiepiscopate in Prague coincided with the peak of Jan Hus's reformist preaching and the subsequent Council of Constance, which condemned Hus. Initially aligned with King Sigismund of Luxembourg, Conrad was pressured to enforce anti-Hussite decrees, which included excommunicating Hussite adherents and interdicting Prague.

Conrad's position became increasingly untenable as the Hussite movement gained popular and noble support. His eventual refusal to publish the papal bull of excommunication against Jan Hus's followers in 1419, and his subsequent decision to join the Hussite Utraquist communion in 1421, marked a dramatic turning point. This act, driven by a complex mix of political pragmatism, personal conviction, and the desire to maintain religious order in Bohemia, led to his excommunication by the papacy and his removal from the Archbishopric of Prague. His defection left a profound vacuum in the Catholic hierarchy of Bohemia, further solidifying the Hussite grip on religious and political power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Conrad of Vechta's defection as Archbishop of Prague to the Hussite cause in 1421 was a dramatic regional event that significantly weakened the Catholic Church's authority in Bohemia and inadvertently strengthened the Hussite movement, contributing to the escalation of the Hussite Wars.
